title: Public Speaking with Confidence
description: Prepare and deliver a talk that people remember. Practice structure, voice, body language, nerves, Q&A, and a complete five-minute capstone presentation.

badge.name: Confident Voice
badge.description: Awarded for completing Public Speaking with Confidence and its final assessment.

outcomes: Analyse an audience and define a clear speaking objective
Structure a talk with a strong opening, body, and close
Use voice, pace, pause, and body language deliberately
Manage nerves with practical preparation routines
Handle questions and recover from mistakes gracefully
Write, rehearse, and deliver a five-minute talk
prerequisites: A topic you care enough about to speak for five minutes
A phone or camera for recording one rehearsal

modules.title: Audience and message
modules.summary: Decide who you are speaking to and what they should remember.

content.text: Public speaking is not performance in a vacuum. It is a relationship with a specific group of people in a specific moment.

Before writing, answer four questions: Who are they? What do they already know? What do they care about? What do I want them to do or feel? The answers determine your examples, your level of detail, and your tone.

rows: Explaining the basics they already know
The recommendation, impact, and next step
A long history of the project

content.title: Write for one person
content.text: Imagine the most important person in the room and speak to them. It keeps the language specific and human, even in a large audience.

content.question: What is the most useful audience question before writing a talk?
options: What do they already know and what do I want them to do?
How many slides can I fit?
What is the room's Wi-Fi password?
content.explanation: Audience knowledge and desired outcome determine the content and level of detail.

content.text: A talk should make one promise and keep it. If you cannot state the promise in a sentence, the audience will not be able to either.
Write a sentence in this shape: 'By the end of this talk, you will know how to [specific thing] so that [benefit].' This becomes your compass when deciding what to include.

rows: You will leave with a 10-minute weekly reset that keeps your priorities visible
You will know the one decision we need to keep the launch on track
You will have a three-step opening that makes your next talk easier to start

content.title: Specific is kind
content.text: A narrow promise respects the audience's time. A broad topic usually means you will either rush or leave people unsure what they gained.

content.question: Which is the strongest speaking promise?
options: By the end, you will know a three-step method for handling difficult questions
content.explanation: It is specific, outcome-oriented, and easy for the audience to remember.

content.text: A reliable structure is: hook, promise, three points, close. It is simple enough to remember under pressure and flexible enough for most talks.

The opening earns attention. The body delivers the promise in two or three clear movements. The close returns to the opening and makes the next step obvious. Do not end with a trail-off or a rushed 'that's it'.

items.title: Hook
items.text: A surprising fact, a short story, a question, or a concrete image. Ten to twenty seconds.

items.title: Promise
items.text: Tell the audience what they will leave with. This gives them a reason to keep listening.

items.title: Point 1
items.text: The first essential idea, with an example or evidence.

items.title: Point 2
items.text: The second idea, connected logically to the first.

items.title: Point 3
items.text: The final idea, often the most important or practical.

items.title: Close
items.text: Return to the opening, restate the promise, and give one clear next step.

content.title: Use signposts
content.text: Say 'First...', 'The second thing...', 'Which brings me to...'. Signposts are not filler; they help the audience build a mental map.

content.question: What should the close do?
options: Return to the opening promise and make the next step clear
Apologise for running out of time
Read the slides one more time
content.explanation: A strong close resolves the talk and makes the takeaway actionable.

modules.title: Delivery
modules.summary: Voice, body, and the nervous system.

content.text: Your voice is an instrument. Volume, pace, pitch, and pause carry meaning that words alone cannot.
Most nervous speakers rush and get quieter. Deliberate pauses are especially powerful: they give the audience time to process, signal that a point matters, and give you time to breathe.

items: Speak one notch slower than feels natural to you.
Pause after the key sentence, not in the middle of it.
Vary pitch to avoid a monotone, but do not force a performance.
Project from the belly, not the throat; breathe low.
Use emphasis on one or two words per sentence, not every word.
Drink water before speaking; avoid shouting to fill a large room without amplification.

content.title: Record a 30-second sample
content.text: Read a paragraph aloud and record it. Listen for pace, volume, and filler words. Most people improve simply by hearing themselves once.

content.question: Why is pause useful in a talk?
options: It gives the audience time to process and adds emphasis
It proves you forgot the words
content.explanation: Strategic silence lets key points land and gives the speaker time to breathe.

content.text: Your body communicates before your first sentence. Standing grounded and looking at people helps the audience trust you and helps you stay present.

Aim for a stable stance, shoulders relaxed, hands available for natural gestures. Move with purpose rather than pacing. Eye contact is not a staring contest; hold one person's gaze for a thought, then move to another part of the room.

items: Stand with both feet grounded.
Keep your hands out of your pockets and away from your face.
Use gestures to show size, sequence, or contrast.
Look at people, not over their heads.
Avoid turning your back to the audience to read the screen.
Smile when it is appropriate; it changes both your face and your nervous system.
Use the clicker in one hand and keep the other free.

content.title: Nervous habits are usually invisible
content.text: The audience cannot feel your heart rate. They notice only what they can see. If your hands shake, hold the clicker with both hands or rest your hands on the lectern.

content.question: What is the best use of eye contact during a talk?
options: Stare at one person the whole time
Hold one person's gaze for a thought, then move around the room
Read every word from the screen
content.explanation: Moving eye contact creates connection without pressure or distraction.

content.text: Nerves are energy. The goal is not to eliminate them but to stop them from steering the talk.

Prepare the opening until it is automatic, because the first thirty seconds are the most nerve-heavy. Breathe slowly before you begin. Arrive early, test the room, and have water nearby. Give yourself a realistic standard: clear and useful, not flawless.

items.title: Prepare more than you think you need
items.text: Know your opening, your three points, and your close cold. Notes can help in the middle.

items.title: Warm up your voice
items.text: Hum, sigh, and say a few sentences aloud before you enter the room.

items.title: Use slow breathing
items.text: Inhale for four counts, exhale for six. Repeat a few times. A longer exhale calms the body.

items.title: Reframe the feeling
items.text: Say 'I am excited' instead of 'I am terrified'. The physical sensation is similar; the interpretation is not.

items.title: Focus on service
items.text: Ask what the audience needs from you. It shifts attention away from self-consciousness.

items.title: Have a recovery plan
items.text: If you lose your place, pause, look at your notes, and say the last point in one sentence. Then continue.

content.title: Do not memorise every word
content.text: A word-for-word script makes one forgotten sentence feel catastrophic. Memorise the structure and the opening; keep the middle flexible.

content.question: What is the most useful preparation for nerves in the first minute?
content.text: No answer needed
options: Memorise the entire talk word for word
Rehearse the opening and first transition until automatic
content.explanation: A confident opening buys time for your nerves to settle and sets the tone.

modules.title: Visuals and story
modules.summary: Make slides and examples support the spoken message.

content.text: A slide should support the speaker, not replace them. If the audience is reading a wall of text, they are not listening to you.
One idea per slide. A sentence title that states the point. A visual or a few short lines. Put the explanation in your spoken words and speaker notes.

rows: A sentence title and one supporting visual
One key point and a concrete example
A simplified chart with the insight in the title
A real image that illustrates the point

content.title: The 3-second test
content.text: Show a slide to someone for three seconds, then hide it. If they cannot say what the main point was, the slide is doing too much.

content.question: What belongs in the speaker's detailed explanation?
options: The speaker notes and spoken delivery
content.explanation: Slides should carry the point; the speaker carries the explanation.

content.text: Stories make ideas memorable. Evidence makes them credible. A strong talk uses both, in the right proportion.

A useful story shape is: a specific person or situation, a complication, and a resolution that illustrates the point. Keep it short. Then support the point with evidence, such as a number, a quote, or a demonstration.

items: Start with a concrete detail, not an abstract concept.
Name the stakes: why did this matter to someone?
Use one story per major point, not five.
After the story, state the connection explicitly.
Use evidence to reinforce, not to overwhelm.
Make sure the story is true or clearly labelled as illustrative.

content.title: Specific beats dramatic
content.text: A small, true detail is more persuasive than a grand claim. 'The support queue waited an extra 14 minutes on Mondays' is stronger than 'customer experience was bad'.

content.question: What should follow a story in a persuasive talk?
options: An explicit connection to the point and supporting evidence
content.explanation: The audience should not have to guess why the story matters.

content.text: A number is only persuasive when the audience can interpret it. Give it scale, comparison, and consequence.

'We saved 8,400 hours' is abstract. 'We saved 8,400 hours, equivalent to four full-time people, which let the team take on two more clients without hiring' is a story. Use comparison, round numbers when precision is not needed, and one number at a time.

rows: Customers wait nearly a full working day for a reply
More than one in three users
About the cost of eight new hires
One fewer error in every 140 orders

content.title: Do not hide uncertainty
content.text: If a number is an estimate, say so. Credibility is lost faster by an overconfident claim than by a clearly labelled assumption.

content.question: What makes a statistic easier to understand?
options: A comparison or consequence that gives it scale
content.explanation: Comparison translates an abstract number into something the audience can interpret.

modules.title: Rehearse and respond
modules.summary: Practice out loud, gather useful feedback, and handle the unexpected.

content.text: Silent rehearsal is not rehearsal. You need to hear the sentences, feel the timing, and practise the transitions between ideas.

Do three passes: one for structure, one for timing, and one for delivery. Use a timer. Record at least one pass on your phone. Watching yourself is uncomfortable, but it is also the fastest feedback loop.

items.title: Structure pass
items.text: Say the whole talk without notes. Notice where you get lost; that is where the structure needs work.

items.title: Timing pass
items.text: Use a timer and adjust the amount of content, not just the speed of your speech.

items.title: Delivery pass
items.text: Focus on pauses, eye contact, and not rushing. Record it.

items.title: Review
items.text: Watch with sound to check pace and filler words; watch muted to check posture and gestures.

items.title: Final dress rehearsal
items.text: Stand up, use the clicker or slides, and do the opening exactly as you will in the room.

content.title: Practise the first 30 seconds more than anything
content.text: A strong opening settles your nerves and sets the audience's expectations. It is worth ten repetitions on its own.

content.question: Why rehearse out loud rather than only in your head?
options: It tests timing, wording, and transitions in a realistic way
It removes the need for notes
content.explanation: Spoken rehearsal exposes awkward phrasing and timing problems that silent reading misses.

content.text: Useful feedback is specific, behavioural, and tied to the audience's experience. 'You were great' is kind but not actionable.

Ask a listener two questions: What was the main point? Where did you lose attention? Then ask for one thing to keep and one thing to change. Avoid collecting ten opinions at once; it will make you second-guess everything.

rows: 'You spoke too fast in the middle'
'I could not tell what you wanted me to do'

content.title: Keep the feedback loop small
content.text: One trusted listener is enough for a short talk. The goal is not to please everyone; it is to make the message land.

content.question: Which feedback is most useful for improving a talk?
options: A specific moment where attention dropped and why
A comment about the room temperature
A list of every filler word
content.explanation: Specific moments give you something concrete to revise.

content.text: Questions are not an interruption to the talk; they are part of it. And mistakes are normal. The audience remembers how you recover, not that you stumbled.

Listen to the whole question before answering. Repeat or paraphrase it for the room if needed. Answer briefly, then check whether you addressed it. If you do not know, say so and offer a follow-up. Do not invent an answer.

items.title: Pause and listen
items.text: Do not start answering while the person is still speaking.

items.title: Clarify if needed
items.text: Ask 'Do you mean X or Y?' if the question is ambiguous.

items.title: Answer the room
items.text: Speak to everyone, not only the questioner.

items.title: Keep it short
items.text: Answer the question, add one supporting detail, then stop.

items.title: Handle the unknown
items.text: Say 'I do not know, but I can find out and follow up.' Write it down so you remember.

content.text: When something goes wrong

items: **Lost your place:** pause, look at your notes, say 'Where I was going was...' and continue.
**Slide fails:** keep talking; describe the point in words. Do not spend minutes fixing technology.
**Said something wrong:** correct it plainly. 'Let me correct that; the figure is 18%, not 80%.'
**Question is hostile:** stay calm, acknowledge the concern, answer the substance, and move on.
**Mind goes blank:** return to your last signpost or your opening promise.

content.title: Plan the difficult question
content.text: Write down the question you least want to be asked. Prepare a calm, honest answer. It will probably not be as bad as you imagine, and you will be ready.

content.question: What is the best response when you do not know an answer?
options: Say you do not know and offer to follow up
content.explanation: Honesty preserves credibility. A clear follow-up commitment is stronger than a made-up answer.

modules.title: Capstone: your five-minute talk
modules.summary: Write it, rehearse it, deliver it, and reflect.

content.text: Your capstone is a five-minute talk on a topic you know or care about. Five minutes is short enough to finish and long enough to require real structure.

Use one sentence for the promise, three points for the body, and a concrete opening and close. Write the outline, not a word-for-word script. Then write the opening and closing sentences exactly; those are worth memorising.

rows: A story, question, or striking detail
What the audience will leave with
Return to promise and next step

content.title: Cut, do not rush
content.text: If the talk is too long, remove a point or an example. Speaking faster is not editing.

content.question: What is the best fix for a talk that runs too long?
content.explanation: Respect the audience's time by editing content, not by compressing delivery.

content.text: Rehearse the capstone at least three times: once for structure, once for time, and once as a full performance.

Record the full performance and watch it. Use the feedback questions from the previous module. Fix the biggest issue first, then rehearse again. Do not keep adding content after the structure is working.

items: The opening makes the audience want to listen.
The promise is stated clearly within the first minute.
There are three distinct points, each with a concrete example.
The close returns to the opening and gives a next step.
The talk fits the time limit with room to breathe.
You can deliver it without reading a script.
Your voice is audible and your pace is steady.
You have a plan for a lost place or a technical failure.

content.title: Rehearse standing up
content.text: Sitting at a desk changes your breathing and energy. Practise in the posture and space you will actually use.

content.question: What should you do after recording your rehearsal?
options: Watch it and identify the single biggest improvement
content.explanation: One focused improvement per rehearsal is more effective than trying to fix everything at once.

content.text: Delivery day is not about being perfect. It is about being present, clear, and useful to the people in the room.

Arrive early, test the setup, breathe, and start with the opening you practised. When questions come, listen fully. When something goes wrong, pause and continue. Afterwards, write down three things that worked and one thing to improve next time.

rows: Stand still, breathe, look at the audience, smile if appropriate
Deliver the memorised opening slowly and clearly
Use signposts, pause after key points, make eye contact
Pause, check notes, restate the last point, continue
Listen, clarify, answer briefly, move on
Thank the audience, note what worked, ask for one improvement

content.title: Confidence is a by-product
content.text: You do not need to feel confident before you speak. You need a clear message, a structure you trust, and enough rehearsal to begin. Confidence often arrives after the first thirty seconds.

content.question: What is the best way to build confidence for future talks?
options: Reflect on what worked and choose one specific improvement
Memorise a new script for every room
content.explanation: Deliberate reflection turns each talk into useful experience for the next one.

finalAssessment.title: Confident Voice assessment
finalAssessment.intro: Answer all eight questions. Score 80% or higher to earn the Confident Voice badge and certificate.

questions.question: What should determine the content and level of detail in a talk?
options: The audience and the desired outcome
questions.explanation: Audience knowledge and the intended outcome shape the talk.

questions.question: What is the strongest speaking promise?
options: I will talk about a topic
By the end, you will know a specific, useful thing
questions.explanation: A specific outcome gives the audience a reason to listen and a way to measure value.

questions.question: What should the close of a talk do?
options: Return to the opening promise and make the next step clear
questions.explanation: A strong close resolves the talk and makes the takeaway actionable.

questions.question: Why are pauses useful?
options: They give the audience time to process and add emphasis
They show you forgot the words
questions.explanation: Strategic silence helps key points land and gives the speaker time to breathe.

questions.question: What is the best way to handle nerves in the first minute?
options: Rehearse the opening until it is automatic
questions.explanation: A strong, practised opening settles nerves and sets the tone.

questions.question: What belongs on a slide?
options: The key point and supporting visual, with detail in your delivery
questions.explanation: Slides support the spoken message; they should not replace the speaker.

questions.question: What is the best response to a question you cannot answer?
options: Say you do not know and offer to follow up
questions.explanation: Honesty preserves credibility, and a follow-up shows responsibility.

questions.question: What is the best way to improve after a talk?
options: Reflect on what worked and choose one specific improvement
Memorise a new script for every room
questions.explanation: Focused reflection turns each talk into useful experience.

questions.question: Which of the following is a best practice covered in this course?
How should you approach a new skill?
questions.explanation: Start with fundamentals and build up.

questions.question: What helps you retain what you learn?
If you get stuck on a lesson, what should you do?
options: Review earlier material and try again
questions.explanation: Reviewing and retrying is part of learning.
